title.en: The mole concept, percent composition and Avogadro's law

text.en: A shopkeeper sells eggs by the dozen and bangles by the pair, because counting one by one is slow. Atoms are far too tiny to count or weigh one by one, so chemists also count them in a bunch, and that bunch is called a mole.

Atoms and molecules are so small that we deal with huge numbers of them, so chemists use a special counting unit called the mole, just as we use a pair or a dozen.
In the SI system one mole is the amount of a substance that contains as many particles as there are atoms in exactly 12 g of carbon-12.
That number was found by experiment and is called Avogadro's number, N A, named after the Italian scientist Amedeo Avogadro; its value is 6.023 x 10^23.
One mole of atoms has a mass in grams equal to its atomic mass, so 16 g of oxygen atoms contain 6.023 x 10^23 atoms.
One mole of molecules has a mass in grams equal to its molecular mass, so 32 g of oxygen gas holds 6.023 x 10^23 oxygen molecules.
Molar volume: one mole of any gas occupies 22.4 litre, or 22400 ml, at STP, which means 273.15 K and 1 atm pressure.
The number of moles is the mass divided by the atomic or molecular mass, and it is also the number of particles divided by 6.023 x 10^23.
Percent composition tells the mass of each element in 100 g of a compound: mass of the element in one formula unit divided by the molecular mass, multiplied by 100.
For water, H2O has molecular mass 18, so hydrogen is 2/18 x 100 = 11.11 percent and oxygen is 16/18 x 100 = 88.89 percent.
For methane, CH4 has mass 16, so carbon is 75 percent and hydrogen is 25 percent; such values help to find empirical and molecular formulae.
In 1811 Avogadro stated his law: equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain an equal number of molecules, so volume is proportional to the number of molecules, V = constant x n.
Check it with H2 + Cl2 giving 2 HCl: one volume plus one volume gives two volumes, so one molecule of hydrogen chloride contains half a molecule of hydrogen and half of chlorine, which shows that molecules split into atoms, in agreement with Dalton's atomic theory.
Avogadro's law also explains Gay-Lussac's law and helps us find the atomicity of gases, for example that hydrogen is diatomic.

problem.en: A sample has 22 g of carbon dioxide, CO2 (C = 12, O = 16). Find the moles, the number of molecules and the volume at STP.

text.en: Molecular mass of CO2 = 12 + 2 x 16 = 44 g per mole.

why.en: You need the molar mass before you can count moles.
One mole of any gas occupies 22.4 L at STP.

prompt.en: Explain what a mole is and how you convert between mass, particles and volume of a gas.

requiredIdeas.en: Mass divided by molar mass gives moles
One mole of a gas is 22.4 L at STP

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking molar volume is 22.4 L for liquids and solids as well
Forgetting to find the molar mass first

points.en: One mole contains 6.023 x 10^23 particles (Avogadro's number).
Moles = mass / molar mass = particles / 6.023 x 10^23.
One mole of any gas occupies 22.4 litre at STP.
Percent composition = mass of element / molecular mass x 100; equal volumes of gases at the same T and P hold equal numbers of molecules.
